title: Garbage and dirty water
summary: With no garbage collection, keep trash in heavy bags inside lidded cans, away from the house, the well and where people sleep; don’t burn it; strain dishwater and scatter it well away from water.

blocks.p: Garbage brings rats, mice, flies and, in much of the Northeast, black bears. Rodents spread disease and can bite people and pets (CDC). Flies carry germs from waste to food and to open water (Oregon State University Extension).

list: Put garbage in heavy-duty garbage bags inside containers with tight lids (New York State Department of Health).
Keep it away from your home and your drinking water well (New York State Department of Health), and away from where people sleep.
Where there are bears, keep the cans in a sturdy building such as a shed or garage (NYS DEC). Keep pet and livestock food indoors and clean grease and food off grills (NYS DEC).
Get trash out of the house as soon as you can, and clean up debris and trash around it (CDC).
Store food and water in thick plastic, glass or metal containers with tight lids, so pests can’t reach them (CDC).
Bagged toilet waste goes in its own can, apart from other garbage (Oregon State University Extension).

blocks.p: In camp, store garbage with the food and every scented item, away from where you sleep.

list: Plan meals so you make as little messy, smelly garbage as possible (Leave No Trace).
In camp, pack out all leftover food, grease and food scraps. Pick up every bit, even orange peel (Leave No Trace).
At home, bag food scraps with the rest of the garbage in a lidded can.
Close every hole in the walls. Some rodents get through holes the size of a dime (CDC).
Catch them with spring-loaded snap traps (CDC).
A dead rodent: wear rubber or plastic gloves, seal it in two plastic bags and throw it away (CDC).

Don’t sweep or vacuum droppings or urine (CDC). Wearing rubber or plastic gloves, spray them with a disinfectant until they are soaked through, and let it soak 5 minutes. Wipe them up with paper towels, and put the towels in a sealed garbage container outdoors (CDC).
Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner (CDC).
A building left empty a long time: air it out for 2 to 3 days before you go in (CDC).
Don’t eat or drink anything rodents may have touched (CDC).

Diapers (baby and adult), sanitary pads and other menstrual products: bag them in heavy-duty 3 to 5 mil black plastic bags (Oregon State University Extension). Never put them in the toilet buckets (Jefferson County). Keep them with the bagged toilet waste until it can be got rid of (Oregon State University Extension).

Needles, lancets and other sharps: put each one straight into a heavy-duty plastic container that stays upright, doesn’t leak and has a tight, puncture-proof lid, such as a plastic laundry detergent bottle. Label it as dangerous waste. Stop at about three-quarters full, close it, and keep it with the bagged waste until it can be got rid of (FDA).

Cleaning up vomit or diarrhea: wear disposable gloves, put the soiled things and the gloves in a plastic trash bag, seal it, and put on new gloves to carry it to a lidded trash can (University of Minnesota Extension). Then wash your hands.
In New York, in normal times: “Burning trash is illegal statewide in all cases.” That includes a burn barrel, a wood stove, a fireplace and an outdoor wood boiler (NYS DEC).
A burn barrel rarely gets hotter than 500°F (260°C). The trash doesn’t burn completely and makes harmful smoke and soot (NYS DEC).
Burning household trash gives off dioxins, fine particles and carbon monoxide. The ash can hold mercury, lead, chromium and arsenic, which garden vegetables take up (EPA).
Half-burned or buried garbage still draws animals (Leave No Trace).

blocks.p: Greywater is the dirty water from washing dishes, hands and people.

list: At home while the sewer still works, pour it down the sink drain, not into the toilet (National Park Service).
When the sewer is not working, or is backing up, don’t pour anything down a drain: water run inside the house can back up into it (West Hants Regional Municipality, Nova Scotia).
With a bucket toilet, use some of it to dilute the pee before you pour it out (Oregon State University Extension).
Strain the rest and scatter it on the ground, away from the house and at least 200 feet (60 m) from wells, springs and streams where you can, as in camp below (Leave No Trace).
Don’t try to treat it to use again (Oregon State University Extension).
Keep it out of a latrine or pit toilet (Sphere handbook).

steps: In camp, carry water at least 200 feet (60 m) from streams and lakes to wash. Never wash in a lake or stream (Leave No Trace).
Use as little soap as you can. New York State land rule in normal times: no soap within 150 feet of water (NYS DEC).
Strain the dirty water through a fine mesh strainer (Leave No Trace).
Scatter it broadly, well away from camp, especially where there are bears (Leave No Trace).
Pack out what is in the strainer with the leftover food (Leave No Trace).

blocks.p: Get rid of dead animals as soon as you can, following your local animal control authority’s guidelines when you can reach them (CDC). Wear gloves.

sources.used: Heavy-duty garbage bags inside containers with tight lids; away from your drinking water well and home

sources.name: CDC, What to Do to Protect Yourself From Animals After a Disaster (August 26, 2026)
sources.used: Rodents spread disease and bite; secure food; throw out trash as soon as you can, in a covered can; clean up debris; store food and water in thick plastic, glass or metal with tight lids; close holes, some rodents fit through a dime-sized hole; snap traps; dead rodent sealed in two plastic bags with rubber or plastic gloves; don’t sweep or vacuum droppings; spray with a disinfectant until thoroughly soaked, soak 5 minutes, remove with paper towels, discard towels outdoors in a sealed garbage container; air out long-abandoned buildings 2 to 3 days; don’t eat or drink what rodents may have touched; dead animals per local animal control (its 1:10 bleach solution, which gives no bleach strength, is not used)

sources.name: NYS DEC, DEC Issues Guidance to Reduce Conflicts with Bears (April 7, 2023); NYS DEC, Be BearWise
sources.used: Secure garbage cans in a sturdy building; store pet and livestock food indoors; clean grease and food from grills; secure food, garbage and recycling

sources.name: Oregon State University Extension Service, Survival Basics: Sanitation and Waste Management (EM 9334, October 2021)
sources.used: Flies carry germs to food and open water; bagged toilet waste stored separately from other garbage; diapers and menstrual products in heavy-duty 3 to 5 mil black bags, disposed of with bagged poo; catch-basin water used to dilute urine, not treated for reuse

sources.name: Jefferson County Department of Emergency Management with Clallam County Sheriff’s Emergency Management, Twin-Bucket Emergency Toilet (updated March 2015)
sources.used: No diapers, sanitary pads or bagged pet waste in the pee or poo buckets

sources.name: University of Minnesota Extension, Step-by-step guide to norovirus cleanup (reviewed 2025)
sources.used: Disposable gloves; soiled items, waste and protective gear in a plastic trash bag, sealed; new gloves to carry the bag to a secure trash container; wash hands

sources.name: NYS DEC, Open Burning
sources.used: “Burning trash is illegal statewide in all cases”, including burn barrels; Part 219 prohibits burning trash in wood stoves, fireplaces and outdoor wood boilers; burn barrels rarely hotter than 500°F, incomplete combustion, harmful smoke and soot

sources.name: US EPA, Backyard Burning: Human Health (archived page)
sources.used: Backyard trash burning releases dioxins, particle pollution, carbon monoxide and other pollutants; ash can contain mercury, lead, chromium and arsenic, which garden vegetables absorb

sources.name: Leave No Trace Center for Outdoor Ethics, Principle 3: Dispose of Waste Properly
sources.used: Plan meals to avoid messy, smelly garbage; pack out all trash, leftover food, grease and micro-trash including orange peels; burning trash never recommended, half-burned or buried garbage still attracts animals; wash 200 feet from streams or lakes, not in them; small amounts of soap; strain with a fine mesh strainer, scatter broadly, well away from camp especially with bears; pack out strainer contents; 200 feet from water sources (applied to scattering greywater at home)

sources.name: NYS DEC, State Land Camping Rules
sources.used: No soap to wash yourself, clothing or dishes within 150 feet of water; carry out what you carry in

sources.name: CDC, How to Safely Clean and Sanitize with Bleach (reviewed August 26, 2026)
sources.used: Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner

sources.name: FDA, Sharps Disposal Containers (content current as of April 28, 2021)
sources.used: Place sharps immediately in a container; if no FDA-cleared container, a heavy-duty plastic household container such as a plastic laundry detergent container, leak-resistant, upright, tight-fitting puncture-resistant lid; labelled to warn of hazardous waste; stop at about three-quarters full

sources.name: West Hants Regional Municipality (Nova Scotia), Municipal Sewage Lift Stations and Power Outages (December 4, 2025)
sources.used: When the sewer is backing up, water run inside the home stays in the internal piping and can back up within the dwelling

sources.used: Pour used dishwater down the sink drain, not into the toilet
